title: Q-learning
objectives: Build a Q-learning agent whose greedy policy matches value iteration on a gridworld.

screens.title: Learn the value of a move
screens.prose: Level 2 needed the slip chances. Now the agent only acts and watches, on the deterministic grid. It keeps a value $Q(s, a)$ for each cell and move, all 0 at first. At row 1, column 4 it moves R into the +1, receiving 0.96, and the episode ends. It moves $Q$ a tenth of the way towards what it saw.
screens.question: What is $Q(\text{r1c4}, R)$ after this update? Give a decimal to 3 places.

hints.text: The episode ends, so the target is the reward, 0.96.
Move a tenth of the way from 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Move a tenth of the way from 0 towards 0.96.

byKey.full: You jumped all the way; the step is 0.1.
byKey.disc: The reward arrives on this step, so it is not discounted.

explain.text: One update: $Q \leftarrow 0 + 0.1 \times 0.96 = 0.096$. Repeated visits pull it towards 0.96, the true value of moving R there, with no model in sight.

screens.title: The Q-learning update
screens.prose: **Q-learning** moves $Q(s, a)$ towards $r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a')$: the reward plus the best value of the next cell, whatever move it will actually take next. At row 2, column 4, $Q(\text{r2c4}, U) = 0.2$. Moving U reaches row 1, column 4, whose largest $Q$ is 0.5.
screens.question: With $\alpha = 0.1$ and $\gamma = 0.9$, what is the new $Q(\text{r2c4}, U)$? Give a decimal to 3 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Build the target, then move a tenth of the way.

byKey.target: That is the target. Move only a tenth of the way to it.
byKey.no-step: You left out the step cost of −0.04.
byKey.no-disc: You left out $\gamma$ on the next value.

explain.text: Target $-0.04 + 0.9 \times 0.5 = 0.41$, so $Q$ rises to 0.221. Because the target takes the max, Q-learning learns the greedy policy's values while it acts epsilon-greedily: it is **off-policy**.

screens.prose: A colleague checks the learned policy by testing `greedy == vi_policy`, cell by cell, where `vi_policy` takes value iteration's first best move in the order U, R, D, L. The check fails at row 4, column 1: Q-learning says R, value iteration says U.

options.text: Nothing is wrong: U and R tie there
Q-learning has not converged at that cell

options.text: Run more episodes until it settles on U
options.why: It may never say U, and it need not: the two moves tie.

options.text: The Q-learning code must have a bug
options.why: A tie broken the other way is not a bug.

Row 3 column 1 and row 4 column 2 are both worth 0.4031.
Equal next values mean equal moves.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the two moves' values.

screens.title: Why start at zero?
screens.prose: Every $Q$ starts at 0, yet every real move costs 0.04 and most true values below row 1 are under 0.6. Early on, a move the agent has never tried still shows 0, while tried moves have dropped below 0.
screens.question: What does that do to the greedy choices early in learning?

options.text: Untried moves look best, so greedy choices explore them
Untried moves look worst, so they are avoided
options.why: Tried moves fall below 0 from the step cost; untried ones stay at 0 and look better.

options.text: Nothing: the start values wash out at once
options.why: They wash out only as moves are tried; until then they steer the choices.

options.text: It biases the final values upwards
options.why: The final values converge to the true ones; the start only shapes early exploring.

hints.text: Compare 0 with a tried move's value early on.
A tried move away from the goal has a value below 0.
So an untried move, still at 0, wins the arg-max.

feedback.correct: Zero is optimistic here, as in level 1: it pushes the agent to try each move.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare 0 with values that have taken a step cost.

explain.text: With a step cost, zero is an optimistic start, like level 1's optimistic estimates. Greedy steps alone then try new moves; the 20% random moves add the rest.

screens.title: Why not the slippery grid?
screens.prose: On the slippery grid, Q-learning with $\alpha = 0.1$ and $\varepsilon = 0.1$ needed 4,400 to 15,250 episodes to match value iteration on 8 of 10 seeds, and failed within 20,000 on the other 2. At row 4, column 3, the best move beats the next by only 0.0073.
screens.question: Why does a constant step struggle here?

options.text: Noisy targets swamp a gap of 0.007 at a constant step
Q-learning needs the slip chances to learn
options.why: It learns from samples; the slips only add noise to the targets.

options.text: Ten per cent exploring is not enough to visit every cell
options.why: Every cell is visited thousands of times; the trouble is how precisely.

options.text: The slippery grid has no single optimal policy
options.why: It has one, with no ties; two cells just have tiny gaps.

hints.text: Each target now depends on where the slip lands.
With $\alpha = 0.1$ an estimate averages roughly the last 10 targets.
That noise is far larger than 0.0073.

feedback.correct: Noise in the target plus a constant step leaves a band wider than the gap.
feedback.generic: Compare the noise with the gap.

explain.text: Convergence needs steps that shrink, with $\sum \alpha_t = \infty$ and $\sum \alpha_t^2 < \infty$ (Sutton and Barto, section 2.7). With a constant 0.1 the estimates keep jiggling, and two moves 0.007 apart keep swapping. So the exit uses the deterministic grid.

screens.title: Q-learning
screens.prose: Q-learning: $$Q(s, a) \leftarrow Q(s, a) + \alpha\,[\,r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a') - Q(s, a)\,],$$ acting epsilon-greedily. It is TD on action values with the greedy target, so it learns the optimal values while acting otherwise. With every pair visited infinitely often and suitably falling steps, it converges to $Q^*$.
screens.question: What makes Q-learning off-policy?

options.text: Its target uses the best next action
It explores at random one step in five
options.why: Exploring is how it acts; off-policy refers to what the target assumes.

options.text: It uses no model of the slip chances
options.why: Model-free and off-policy are different ideas.

options.text: It stores values of actions, not states
options.why: SARSA stores action values too and is on-policy (lesson 12).

feedback.correct: The max in the target evaluates the greedy policy whatever the agent actually does.

screens.title: Learning to quote from a simulator
screens.prose: A desk trains a quoting rule in an order-flow simulator. In state "flat, wide market" it tightens its quote, earns £0.50, and lands in "long one, quiet", whose best action is worth £2.00. $Q(\text{flat wide}, \text{tighten})$ was £0; $\alpha = 0.2$, $\gamma = 0.95$.
screens.question: What is the updated $Q$, in pounds? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Move a fifth of the way from 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Build the target, then move a fifth of the way.

byKey.target: That is the target; the step is 0.2.
byKey.no-disc: You took $\alpha = 0.2$ of 2.50: discount the next value first.
byKey.reward: You used the reward alone; add the discounted next value.

explain.text: The target is £2.40 and a fifth of it gives £0.48. A simulator supplies the samples cheaply; whether the learned rule survives real flow is the question lesson 12 raises.

ideas: Q-learning keeps $Q(s, a)$ and moves it towards $r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a')$ after every step, with no model.
Its max target makes it off-policy: it learns the greedy policy's values while acting epsilon-greedily. On the deterministic grid its greedy policy was optimal for seeds 0 to 49 after 200 episodes.
Check a learned policy against optimal sets, since moves can tie. Unvisited cells keep their initial values, and noisy targets with a constant step can blur small gaps.

formula.name: Q-learning
formula.tex: Q(s, a) \leftarrow Q(s, a) + \alpha\,[\,r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a') - Q(s, a)\,]
formula.note: At a terminal step the target is $r$; converges to $Q^*$ when every pair is tried often and steps shrink suitably.

summary.trap: Checking a learned policy by one arg-max against value iteration's: in tied cells both moves are optimal.

options.text: The greedy, optimal policy's
The epsilon-greedy policy it follows
